title: The Great Barrier Reef
summary: The Great Barrier Reef off Australia is the world's largest coral reef system, so big it can be seen from space.
poll: A place that is home to thousands of different kinds of sea life deserves special protection.

versions.title: The Great Barrier Reef
versions.text:
A giant reef sits off the coast. It is the Great Barrier Reef. It is the biggest reef on Earth.

The reef is not one thing. It has many small reefs. It has small islands too.

The reef is big. You can see it from space. Few things are that big.

Many animals live on the reef. Fish of every color swim there. Sharks live there. Turtles live there too.

Tiny coral build the reef. Each one makes a cup. The cups pile up high.

The reef is in danger now. Hot seas can turn coral white. People work to help this place.

The reef is so huge. It can be seen from space! Very few things on Earth are that big.

Tiny coral build this reef, bit by bit. Each soft coral makes a hard cup. Over time, these cups pile up high.

Sadly, the reef faces danger today. When the sea gets hot, coral can turn white. Scientists work hard to protect this place.

versions.title: The Great Barrier Reef
versions.text:
A huge reef system lies off the coast of Australia, within the warm waters of the Coral Sea, known as the Great Barrier Reef, recognized as the biggest coral reef system found anywhere on Earth.

The reef is not a single, solid structure. It is composed of almost 3,000 smaller reefs, plus about 900 islands, together covering an area larger than many whole countries. These pieces stretch more than 2,300 kilometers along the coast of Queensland, forming an enormous marine ecosystem.

The reef is so vast that it can actually be seen from outer space, making it one of the very few living structures on Earth large enough for astronauts to recognize. Almost no other living structure grows large enough to be identified from such a great distance.

An astonishing variety of animals live within this one connected ecosystem. Fish of every color dart among the branching coral, while sharks, turtles, dugongs, and giant clams also live there. Researchers are still finding and naming new creatures here every year. Scientists estimate that the reef holds many thousands of species.

Tiny coral polyps build this entire massive formation, bit by tiny bit, over an immense stretch of time. Each soft polyp builds a hard limestone skeleton, and when it dies, new polyps grow directly on top of its remains. Over thousands of years, these layers pile up, shaped by changes in sea level.

Sadly, the reef faces real danger today, much of it tied to a warming and increasingly acidic sea. When the surrounding sea stays too hot for too long, stressed coral can turn pale white and grow dangerously weak, and it may even starve.

Scientists, local communities, and the government are now collaborating on long-term plans to protect this marine wonder so that it can thrive for generations to come.

versions.title: The Great Barrier Reef
versions.text:
Off the coast of Australia, within the warm waters of the Coral Sea, lies a truly colossal reef system known as the Great Barrier Reef, widely recognized as the largest coral reef formation found anywhere on Earth, far surpassing any rival system in total area.

The reef is not a single, solid structure at all. Rather, it is composed of almost 3,000 smaller individual reefs, along with roughly 900 islands and sandy cays scattered across the ocean, together occupying an area larger than many entire countries. These pieces stretch for more than 2,300 kilometers along the Queensland coastline, a scale that is genuinely difficult for most visitors to grasp. The Great Barrier Reef Marine Park, set up to manage the region, covers an area of more than 344,000 square kilometers.

The reef is so vast that it can actually be seen from outer space, making it one of the very few living formations astronauts can recognize without any instruments. Almost no other living structure grows large enough to be seen from so far away.

An astonishing variety of animals make their homes within this single, interconnected ecosystem. Fish of every color dart among the branching coral formations, while sharks, sea turtles, dugongs, and giant clams also make the reef their home. Scientists estimate that the reef supports extraordinary biodiversity, with many thousands of known species.

Tiny coral polyps, often only a few millimeters wide, constructed this entire massive formation, bit by tiny bit, over an immense span of geological time. Each soft polyp builds a hard limestone skeleton around its own body, and when a polyp dies, successive generations grow directly on top of its remains. Over thousands of years, countless layers of skeletons and fine sediment built up together, shaped by repeated changes in sea level across many ice ages.

Sadly, the reef faces real threats today, many connected to a warming and increasingly acidic ocean, since reef-building coral is especially vulnerable to even modest shifts in water temperature. When the sea remains unusually hot for extended periods, stressed coral can turn pale white and grow dangerously weak.

Scientists, local communities, and the Australian government are now collaborating on long-term conservation efforts, including a dedicated marine park established decades ago, to protect this remarkable natural heritage site for future generations.

Rather, it is composed of almost 3,000 smaller individual reefs, along with roughly 900 islands and sandy cays scattered across the ocean, together occupying an area larger than many entire countries. These pieces stretch for more than 2,300 kilometers along the Queensland coastline, a scale that is genuinely difficult for most visitors to grasp without experiencing it firsthand. Almost no other living structure on the planet grows large enough to be identified from such an extraordinary distance.

An astonishing variety of animals make their homes within this single, interconnected ecosystem. Fish of every color dart among the branching coral formations, while sharks, sea turtles, dugongs, and giant clams also make the reef their home. Scientists estimate that the reef supports extraordinary biodiversity, including more than 1,500 species of fish and over 400 types of coral alone, a concentration of life rarely matched elsewhere in the ocean.

Tiny coral polyps, often only a few millimeters wide, constructed this entire massive formation, bit by tiny bit, over an immense span of geological time. Each soft polyp builds a hard limestone skeleton around its own body, and when a polyp dies, successive generations grow directly on top of its remains. When the sea remains unusually hot for extended periods, stressed coral expels its algae, turns pale white, and grows dangerously weak. Major bleaching events have struck the reef multiple times in recent decades, alarming scientists worldwide.

Scientists, local communities, and the Australian government are now collaborating on long-term conservation efforts, including a dedicated marine park established decades ago, to protect this remarkable natural heritage site for future generations.

versions.title: The Great Barrier Reef
versions.text:
Off the northeastern coast of Australia, within the warm waters of the Coral Sea, lies a truly colossal reef system known as the Great Barrier Reef, widely recognized as the largest coral reef formation found anywhere on Earth, far surpassing any rival system in total area by an enormous margin.

The reef is not a single, solid structure at all. Rather, it is composed of almost 3,000 smaller individual reefs, along with roughly 900 islands and sandy cays scattered across the ocean, collectively occupying an area larger than many entire countries combined. Together, these pieces stretch for more than 2,300 kilometers along the Queensland coastline, forming an enormous and intricate marine ecosystem that remains visible even from high in the air, let alone from the ground, a scale that is genuinely difficult for most visitors to fully grasp without experiencing it firsthand.

The reef is so vast that it can actually be seen from outer space, making it one of the very few living formations on Earth large enough for astronauts to recognize without any specialized instruments whatsoever. Astronauts orbiting high above the planet have repeatedly photographed its pale, winding shapes against the deep blue ocean below, since almost no other living structure on the planet grows large enough to be identified from such an extraordinary distance.

An astonishing variety of animals make their homes within this single, interconnected ecosystem. Fish of every imaginable color dart among the branching coral formations, while sharks, sea turtles, dugongs, and giant clams also make the reef their home, alongside countless smaller invertebrates that researchers continue cataloguing to this day. Scientists estimate that the reef supports extraordinary biodiversity, with many thousands of known species and likely many more awaiting formal scientific description, a concentration of life rarely matched elsewhere in the world's oceans and often compared to the richness of a tropical rainforest.

Tiny coral polyps, often only a few millimeters wide, constructed this entire, massive formation, bit by tiny bit, over an immense span of geological time. Each soft polyp builds a hard limestone skeleton around its own body, and when a polyp eventually dies, successive generations of new polyps grow directly on top of its remains. Over thousands of years, countless layers of these skeletons and fine sediment accumulated on top of one another, and this slow, steady process of accumulation is precisely how such a gigantic reef formed; the oldest layers beneath today's living coral are many thousands of years old, while the broader geological foundation beneath the reef stretches back far longer still, shaped by repeated changes in sea level across many successive ice ages.

Sadly, the reef faces very real and mounting threats today, many connected to a warming and increasingly acidic ocean, since reef-building corals are especially vulnerable to even modest, short-term shifts in water temperature. When the surrounding sea remains unusually hot for extended periods, stressed corals expel their resident algae, turn pale white, and grow dangerously weak, sometimes starving entirely if the heat does not ease in time. Scientists, local communities, and the Australian government are now collaborating on serious, long-term conservation efforts, including a dedicated marine park established decades ago, to protect this remarkable natural heritage site so that it can continue thriving for generations still to come.

MID.prompt: Explain what makes the Great Barrier Reef such a unique ecosystem, and why it now faces danger. Use evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained what makes the reef unique.
I described the danger it faces.
I used evidence from the article.
MID.modelAnswer: The Great Barrier Reef is a unique marine ecosystem because it is not one single structure but almost 3,000 smaller reefs and hundreds of islands that together stretch over 2,000 kilometers, forming the largest coral reef system on Earth. It supports an enormous variety of species, including fish of every color, sharks, sea turtles, and giant clams, all living together in a habitat so large it can be seen from outer space. However, the reef now faces danger because when the surrounding sea stays unusually hot for too long, stressed coral turns white and grows weak, which is why scientists and the Australian government are now working on long-term conservation efforts to protect it.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how the Great Barrier Reef's massive scale and biodiversity make it globally significant, and why its vulnerability to ocean warming matters. Use evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained the reef's scale and biodiversity.
I connected its vulnerability to ocean warming.
I supported my ideas with evidence from the article.
HIGH.modelAnswer: The Great Barrier Reef is globally significant because of its extraordinary scale: composed of almost 3,000 smaller reefs and roughly 900 islands stretching more than 2,300 kilometers, it is large enough to be recognized from outer space, a distinction shared by almost no other living formation on Earth. Its biodiversity is equally remarkable, supporting many thousands of species, including fish, sharks, sea turtles, dugongs, and giant clams, a concentration of marine life the article compares to a tropical rainforest. This scale and biodiversity make the reef's vulnerability especially significant, since reef-building corals are highly sensitive to even modest shifts in water temperature; when the sea stays unusually hot for too long, stressed corals expel their algae, turn white, and can starve. Because this fragile, ancient formation took thousands of years to build from coral skeletons and sediment, and supports so much of the ocean's biodiversity, protecting it through long-term conservation efforts matters not just for Australia but for the health of the world's oceans as a whole.
